title: 1.4.22 Module 1.4 Quiz
description: Eight multiple-choice questions on purpose-driven languages, levels of abstraction, and the three paradigms. Checked instantly.

questions.question: SQL is a language built for asking questions of a database. Why could you not use it to build a web page?
options: SQL is too old to run in a modern browser
SQL was designed for one job: asking a database questions, and has no way to build an interface
SQL runs too slowly to keep up with a web page
SQL can only be used by professional programmers
questions.explanation: Languages are purpose driven. SQL does its one job well and simply has no way to build the parts of a page you click on: it is not a matter of age or speed.

questions.question: Which of these best describes a LOW-level language?
options: One that hides hardware details so you say what should happen, not how
One that only beginners use
One that makes you describe the work in terms the hardware handles directly
One that can only run on older computers
questions.explanation: Low-level means close to the hardware: you handle details like where each value sits in memory. The first option describes a high-level language.

questions.question: What do you gain by choosing a high-level language like JavaScript?
options: You write it faster, and whole categories of mistake become impossible
The program always runs faster than a low-level one would
Complete control over which memory addresses hold your values
It is the only kind of language a browser can run
questions.explanation: High-level buys writing speed and fewer mistakes; low-level buys run speed and control. Which one wins depends on which resource is scarce for that project.

questions.question: What is a programming paradigm?
options: The punctuation rules a particular language uses
Another word for a programming language
The program you type your code into
An approach to organising and structuring code
questions.explanation: Definition 1.4.2: a paradigm is an approach to organising and structuring code: how a program is broken into pieces and how those pieces fit together. It is not a language, and it is not syntax.

questions.question: Structured programming says every program can be built from just three structures. Which three?
options: Input, processing and output
Sequence, selection and repetition
Variables, functions and objects
Design, development and testing
questions.explanation: Sequence, selection and repetition, and nothing more exotic. There is no fourth structure waiting in a later chapter.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of SELECTION?
options: Printing three lines one after another
Repeating a step until something becomes true
Choosing between two paths depending on a condition
Giving a group of steps a name so you can reuse it
questions.explanation: Selection is the choice: `if` and `switch`. Doing things in order is sequence; doing something more than once is repetition.

questions.question: What is the difference between procedural and object-oriented programming?
options: Object-oriented is newer, so it is always the better choice
Procedural code cannot use variables
Procedural keeps data and behaviour separate; object-oriented bundles them together
Object-oriented programs do not need to store any data
questions.explanation: That separation is the whole contrast. Procedural is a sequence of steps acting on data held elsewhere; object-oriented is objects that hold their own data and the behaviour that works on it. Neither is better in general.

questions.question: A function written in the functional style always gives the same answer for the same input, and changes nothing outside itself. Why does that make it easier to test?
options: Functional programs are shorter, so there is less to test
You can check it on its own: there is no setup first, and nothing else can affect the answer
Functional code cannot contain bugs
The language tests functional code for you automatically
questions.explanation: Because it depends on nothing but its inputs, you never have to ask what else happened first. That is exactly what makes it checkable on its own.
